subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Textile artists and the formal elements

questions.q: In the batik technique, which material is applied to fabric to resist the dye?
questions.explain: Batik uses molten wax as a resist so the waxed areas stay their original colour when the fabric is dyed.

questions.q: Which embroidery stitch is made up of a series of crossed diagonal stitches forming X shapes?
questions.explain: Cross stitch is worked as pairs of diagonal stitches that cross to form small X shapes, often on a grid.

questions.q: On a loom, in which direction do the warp threads run?
options: Woven over and under by hand only
In a spiral from the centre
questions.explain: The warp threads run lengthwise and are held taut on the loom, while the weft is woven across them.

questions.q: Which of the following is a natural fibre obtained from an animal?
questions.explain: Wool is a natural fibre from sheep, whereas polyester, nylon and acrylic are synthetic (man-made) fibres.

questions.q: The traditional natural dye indigo produces which colour?
questions.explain: Indigo is a natural dye long used to produce blue colours, famously in denim and batik.

questions.q: The British textile designer William Morris is most closely associated with which movement?
questions.explain: William Morris was a leading figure of the Arts and Crafts movement, known for patterned printed textiles such as 'Strawberry Thief'.

questions.q: Which formal element describes the surface quality of a textile, such as smooth, rough or fluffy?
questions.explain: Texture is the formal element that refers to surface quality, which can be both actual (felt) and visual (implied).

questions.q: In screen printing, ink is pushed through the mesh screen using which tool?
questions.explain: A squeegee is drawn across the screen to force ink through the open areas of the mesh onto the fabric.

questions.q: Why is wax applied to specific areas of fabric before dyeing in batik?
options: The wax resists the dye, keeping those areas their original colour
The wax speeds up how quickly the dye is absorbed
The wax permanently changes the fibre into a synthetic one
The wax makes the whole fabric a single flat colour
questions.explain: Wax acts as a resist, blocking the dye so the covered areas remain undyed and create the pattern.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of using a mordant when dyeing textiles?
options: To fix the dye to the fibre and improve colour fastness
To bleach the fabric white before dyeing
To soften the fabric so it is easier to fold
questions.explain: A mordant bonds the dye to the fibre, helping the colour last and resist washing out.

questions.q: Why can wool be felted into a solid fabric while cotton cannot?
options: Wool fibres have tiny scales that interlock under heat, moisture and agitation
Wool fibres are made of plastic that melts together
Cotton fibres are far longer than wool fibres
Cotton dissolves completely when it gets wet
questions.explain: The microscopic scales on wool fibres catch and lock together when agitated with heat and moisture, forming felt.

questions.q: What is the key difference between appliqué and embroidery?
options: Appliqué attaches cut fabric shapes onto a background, while embroidery decorates with stitched thread
Appliqué is done only by machine, while embroidery is only ever done by hand
Appliqué uses dye, while embroidery uses wax resist
There is no difference; the two terms mean the same thing
questions.explain: Appliqué stitches pieces of fabric onto a ground cloth, whereas embroidery builds decoration from thread stitches alone.

questions.q: How does repeating a single motif across a length of fabric mainly affect the design?
options: It creates pattern and a sense of rhythm
It removes all colour from the design
It changes the fibre from natural to synthetic
questions.explain: Repeating a motif produces pattern, and the regular repetition gives the design visual rhythm.

questions.q: In tie-dye, why do the tightly bound areas of fabric stay lighter or undyed?
options: The binding stops the dye from penetrating those areas
The binding attracts extra dye to those areas
The binding turns the dye a different colour
The binding removes the fibre completely
questions.explain: Tying or binding acts as a resist, preventing dye from reaching the compressed fabric so it stays pale.

questions.q: The American artist Faith Ringgold is best known for which kind of textile work?
options: Story quilts that combine painting, fabric and narrative text
Woven woollen carpets in geometric patterns
questions.explain: Faith Ringgold is celebrated for her story quilts, which combine painted images, pieced fabric and written narrative.

questions.q: Why might a designer choose polyester rather than cotton for a hard-wearing outdoor banner?
options: Polyester is stronger, more durable and less likely to shrink or rot
Polyester is a natural fibre grown from a plant
Polyester cannot be printed on at all
questions.explain: As a synthetic fibre, polyester is strong, durable and resistant to shrinking and rotting, suiting outdoor use.

questions.q: A student needs to print many identical, crisp copies of the same motif quickly along a long piece of fabric. Which technique is most suitable?
options: A single line of hand embroidery
questions.explain: Screen printing uses one stencil screen to repeat identical, sharp images rapidly across the fabric.

questions.q: A student wants a soft, graduated blend of colour that fades from dark to light along a hanging, with no sharp edges. Which method best achieves this?
questions.explain: Gradually immersing the fabric in dye (dip dyeing) creates a smooth ombre gradient from dark to light.

questions.q: A student wants to emphasise strong actual texture in a woven wall hanging. Which approach would work best?
options: Layering different fabrics and adding raised, three-dimensional stitching
Printing a flat photograph onto smooth cotton
Dyeing the whole piece one even colour
Drawing the pattern with a fine pencil only
questions.explain: Combining varied fabrics with raised stitching builds real, tactile texture that can be felt as well as seen.

questions.q: A student is planning a piece using natural plant dyes and wants the colour to last well after washing. What should they do to the fibre first?
options: Treat it with a mordant before dyeing
Coat it in molten wax over the whole surface
Soak it in bleach and leave it to dry
Iron it at the highest heat setting
questions.explain: Pre-treating the fibre with a mordant helps natural dyes bond and resist fading when the fabric is washed.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Art & Design (0400) syllabus; Textiles
